newsitem.title: THAILAND: Over 2,000 in fray in Thailand general election.
newsitem.headline: Over 2,000 in fray in Thailand general election.

text.p: Registrations closed on Friday for candidates in Thailand's November 17 general election, with the parties led by a former prime minister and an ex-army chief emerging as major rivals.
The parties of former Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai and ambitious ex-army chief Chavalit Yongchaiyudh fielded the most candidates for the election after a five-day registration period, officials said.

Chuan's Democrat Party, which led a coalition government during 1992-1995, fielded about 375 candidates, while about 300 will run under the banner of Chavalit's well-financed New Aspiration Party (NAP).
The NAP has been the main beneficiary of defections from caretaker premier Banharn Silpa-archa's Chart Thai party.
Leaders of the two rival parties said this week they each hoped to win 120-130 seats in the 393-seat lower House of Representatives to get a mandate to lead the next coalition.
Officials said about 2,100 politicians have entered the contest for lower house seats.

The Democrat Party, aiming to win 45-50 seats in its stronghold in southern Thailand, campaigned mainly on a platform that it had the best economic team to boost a slowing Thai economy that is projected to grow this year at its slowest pace in a decade.

Chuan's party led in the most recent private polls of businessmen and urban voters. Former finance minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and deputy premier Supachai Panichpakdi are running in Bangkok as Democrats.

Chavalit's NAP saw a sharply brighter prospect of leading the next government after its ranks were boosted by politicians defecting from other parties. It hopes to capture up to 80 of 137 seats at stake in the north east.
The NAP has about 119 incumbent members of parliament contesting under its banner against 97 parliament deputies running as Democrats.
The Democrats have charged rivals of vote buying and warned Thais that parties with big campaign war chests would be corrupt and later try to cash in on their investment.
NAP denied of being involved in vote buying.
"Rural folks do not object to vote buying. With the going trend, the Democrats would probably lose out to the NAP. But that does not guarantee Chavalit the premiership," said one financial analyst.

Chavalit, in a move to shore up his trailing popularity among the business community, told foreign investors on Thursday that his government, if elected, would pursue fiscal discipline. He said he was not an advocate of big military spending on arms.
Chavalit, a former army general, had in the past supported the Thai military acquiring submarines and satellites.
Another former prime minister attempting a political comeback is Chatichai Choonhavan, 74, who was ousted from office by a military coup in early 1991.
Analysts expected Chatichai's Chart Pattana Party to win about 60 seats to become a crucial bloc that both the Democrats and NAP need to ally with to form a viable government.
Chatichai told Thais if his party was elected they could see an economic boom similar to one Thailand experienced in the late 1980s and early 1990s when he was prime minister.
